title: Kesho: the -ta- slot and plans yet to happen
goal: Talk about plans, make arrangements, and use the one Swahili slot whose negative changes nothing but the prefix.
bekal: its negative: *sitakwenda* — same slot, same ending
*nitakuwa* and *kutakuwa na* for "will be" and "there will be"

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Mipango ya likizo
dialogs.intro: The long holidays are just a week away. Juma wants to know Budi's plans.

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.id: What are you going to do over the holidays?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'm going to Arusha. I'll see the Serengeti!

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.id: That's awesome! Who are you going with?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nitakwenda na Amina. Tutakaa huko siku tano.
lines.id: I'm going with Amina. We'll stay there five days.
lines.literal: I-will-go with Amina. we-will-stay there days five.

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.text: Mtaona wanyama wengi: simba, tembo, twiga, pundamilia.
lines.id: You'll see lots of animals: lions, elephants, giraffes, zebras.
lines.literal: you(pl)-will-see animals many: lions, elephants, giraffes, striped-donkeys.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'll take tons of photos! Aren't you coming?

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.text: Sitaweza. Nitafanya kazi wiki ijayo, hoteli itakuwa na wageni wengi.
lines.id: I can't. I'm working next week, and the hotel will be full of guests.
lines.literal: I-not-will-be-able. I-will-do work week which-comes, hotel it-will-have guests many.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: What a shame. We'll bring you back a present.

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.id: Thanks so much! When are you leaving?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: We leave Friday morning, God willing.

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.id: Have a good trip! When are you coming back?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tutarudi Jumatano ijayo. Nitakuwa na habari nyingi!
lines.id: We're back next Wednesday. I'll have lots of stories!
lines.literal: we-will-return Wednesday which-comes. I-will-have news many!

notes: **Kupiga literally means "to hit", and it's the most versatile verb in Swahili.** *Kupiga picha* (to take a photo), *kupiga simu* (to phone), *kupiga kelele* (to shout), *kupiga mswaki* (to brush your teeth), *kupiga deki* (to mop), *kupiga soga* (to chat). If you forget a verb, try *kupiga* — your odds aren't bad.

**Ijayo means "the coming one".** *Wiki ijayo* (next week), *mwaka ujao* (next year), *Jumatano ijayo* (next Wednesday). Its form follows the noun class — *i-* for *wiki*, *u-* for *mwaka* — and its opposite is *iliyopita* (last, past).

**Mungu akipenda = God willing.** Literally "if God likes", and it's used exactly where Muslims say *inshallah* — a form that is itself widely used on the coast. The *-ki-* form meaning "if" is covered fully in unit 19.
**Safari njema means "have a good trip".** *Njema* is the N-class form of *-ema* (good). Its cousins: *usiku mwema* (good night), *siku njema* (have a nice day), *karibu tena*.
**Zawadi means a present or souvenir**, and bringing a *zawadi* home from a trip is a strong custom in East Africa — however small. The sentence: *Nimekuletea zawadi kidogo*.

grammars.title: The -ta- slot: the easiest of all
body: The future is made with the **-ta-** slot, and it's the only slot whose negative **changes nothing** except the subject prefix. No ending changes, no slot gets swapped.
after: One-syllable verbs keep their *ku-* in both forms: *nitakula*, *sitakula*, *nitakunywa*, *sitakunywa*, *nitakuja*, *sitakuja*, *nitakwenda*, *sitakwenda*.
You've been using this slot since unit 1 without realizing it: **tutaonana** — "we will see each other", i.e. see you later.

For "will be" and "there will be": *nitakuwa mwalimu* (I'll be a teacher), *kutakuwa na sherehe* (there'll be a party), *hakutakuwa na mvua* (there won't be any rain), *nitakuwa na muda* (I'll have time).

grammars.title: Four slots, one table
body: With this unit you hold the whole A1 tense system of Swahili. This page is worth bookmarking — you'll come back to it again and again.
after: The *hu-* row is a small extra you haven't met yet: it marks **a habit that repeats with no time limit**, and unusually it goes **in place of** the subject prefix, not after it. *Husoma kila siku* = (she) reads every day. It turns up most in general truths and proverbs: *Watoto hupenda pipi* (children love sweets).
The negative prefixes used throughout this table are the same six: *si-*, *hu-*, *ha-*, *hatu-*, *ham-*, *hawa-*. You've been using them since unit 2 as *sina*, *huna*, *hana*.
Notice that **the root is never touched** anywhere in the table. That's the promise this book's introduction made: you don't memorize twenty forms of one verb, you snap on slots.

sections.title: Wanyama — and why Simba is called Simba

blocks.text: You may know more East African animal names than you think — some have been on screen for a long time.

*Simba* really does mean lion, and *rafiki* really does mean friend — two words millions of people learned from one film without realizing they were hearing Swahili. The same goes for *hakuna matata*, a real phrase that people really use, though in daily life you'll more often hear *hakuna shida* and *hakuna noma*.

*Safari* itself is a Swahili word the whole world has borrowed — and it doesn't mean "watching animals" but **any journey**. Taking the bus to the next town is a *safari* too. For "wildlife tourism", the better phrase is *utalii wa wanyama*.

sections.title: Kesho, wiki ijayo — marking what's ahead

blocks.text: **A note on promises.** *Mungu akipenda* or *Inshallah* at the end of a plan isn't mere politeness — it's part of how people talk, and saying it makes your sentence sound natural. But it also says something about how plans are seen: what hasn't happened yet isn't certain, and there's no point pretending otherwise.
Useful sentences for making arrangements: *Tutaonana kesho* (see you tomorrow), *Nitakupigia simu* (I'll call you), *Utakuwa huru lini?* (when will you be free?), *Nitakujulisha* (I'll let you know).

exercises.prompt: Choose the right slot (-na-, -li-, -me-, -ta-), then write the sentence.
items: Tomorrow I'll go to the market. → ____
Yesterday I went to the market. → ____
I'm at the market now (I'm shopping). → ____
Next week we'll stay in Arusha. → ____
What are you going to do over the holidays?
We won't come back on Friday.
There will be a big party.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: Nitasoma. — Atakuja kesho. — Tutakwenda Arusha. — Watakula pilau. — Utafanya kazi. — Kutakuwa na sherehe.
Sitakwenda. — Hatakuja. — Hatutaweza. — Hawatarudi. — Hutakula. — Gari halitafika.
Kesho nitakwenda sokoni. — Jana nilikwenda sokoni. — Nimefika sokoni. — Ninanunua sokoni sasa. — Wiki ijayo tutakaa Arusha.
Utafanya nini likizo? — Nitakwenda Arusha. — Mtaondoka lini? — Hatutarudi Ijumaa. — Kutakuwa na sherehe kubwa. — Safari njema!
Utafanya nini likizo? — Nitasafiri kwenda Arusha. — Mtaondoka lini? — Mtaona wanyama wengi. — Tutaondoka Ijumaa, Mungu akipenda.
